gallery.artist: Henry M. Hyde, photo probably provided by the Illinois Tunnel Company
gallery.credit: Rapid Transit in New York and Other Great Cities, Chamber of Commerce of the State of New York, 1905; page 244.  This photo appeared earlier in Henry M. Hyde, People or Freight Underground, The Technical World, Vol. 1, No. 5 (July 1904); page 532.
gallery.description: Original captions: Rapid Transit:  "FREIGHT TRAIN AT STREET INTERSECTION -- CHICAGO"; The Technical World: "FREIGHT TRAINS AT STREET INTERSECTION." Captions from an almost identical photo identify this as a view looking north through the intersection of State and Randolph streets and identify the man driving the left locomotive as Superintendent George W. Jackson.  Two locomotives on the Morgan third-rail rack trackage of the Illinois Tunnel Company.  The locomotives were built by the Goodman Equipment Corporation.  This is a composite of scans of 4 different copies of 'Rapid Transit in New York', scaled to match and overlayed to mute the moiré patterns in the scan and sharpen the result.

gallery.title: File:TunnelCoalDelivery.jpg
gallery.artist: Special Committe on Recognition of Members of the Chamber on the Rapid Transit Commission.  No attribution of photo credit is given, but the photo was probably provided by the Illinois Tunnel Company.
gallery.description: Original caption:  "TYPICAL DISTRIBUTING STATION -- CHICAGO."  Newly constructed coal delivery facilities in the basement of a building in the Chicago Loop served by the Illinois Tunnel Company (later, the Chicago Tunnel Company).  Bruce Moffat identifies the location as "a building on the north side of Monroe between Wells and LaSalle that was occupied by the Illinois Telephone Construction Company."

gallery.title: File:ChicagoTunnelFields.png
gallery.artist: No attribution.  Photo probably provided by Illinois Tunnel Company or from en:Marshall Field's.
gallery.description: Original caption: "ENTRANCE TO MARSHALL FIELD & COMPANY'S TUNNEL BASEMENT, SHOWING TYPE OF ELECTRIC MOTOR USED".  This photo also appears in Bruce Moffat, Forty Feet Below, Interurban Press, 1982, page 27, with the caption: "... Jeffrey Locomotive 130, looking toward State Street just after the floor was lowered to meet the tunnel grade."  This photo is obviously posed -- there are no overhead wires in place yet to power the locomotive.

gallery.title: File:IllinoisTunnelConstruction.jpg
gallery.artist: George W. Jackson  (died 1922)
gallery.description: Original captions:  Mines and Minerals: "Lateral Tunnel Under Construction."  Page's: "LATERAL CONDUIT UNDER CONSTRUCTION."  Western: "Lateral Conduit Under Construction" and inscribed on the photo, "[Illegible] 9-15-02 Ill. Telephone & Telegraph Co -- Construction Methods --".  This image is a composite from 3 published sources in order to eliminate artifacts from both printing and scanning.  For scale, note that the track in the tunnel is 14-inch gauge.

gallery.title: File:IllinoisTunnelMap1904.png
gallery.artist: Illinois Tunnel Company
gallery.description: Title at top of map:  "Chicago's Business District Showing Railroad Terminals"  Key:  Red lines - "Illinois Tunnel Company's Tunnels - Over 20 Miles Completed"; Hatched area - "Business District"; Green - "Rail Road Property".  Title at bottom of map:  "Illinois Tunnel Company - Drawing No. 460".  Note that the large red blotch has no explanation.  Neither the river crossing adjacent to this blotch nor the tunnels parallel to the river north toward Union Station were ever completed.

gallery.title: File:IllinoisTunnelShaft7.jpg
gallery.artist: George W. Jackson (died 1922)
gallery.description: Original Captions:  Western: "Fig. 10.  Elevator House to lift the excavated clay that it may be dumped into wagons to be hauled away to the Lake Front."; Page's:  "Fig 6: ELEVATOR HOUSE Used for lifting the excavated clay so that it may be dumped into waggons to be hauled away to the Lake Front."; Mines:  "Fig 9.  Elevator house."  Additional inscription on the margin of the photo as shown in Western and Mines: "9-15-02 Illinois Telephone & Telegraph Co. Filling Wagons at Shaft No. 7"  This image is a composite of all three published versions in order to eliminate printing and scanning artifacts.  The table of construction shafts in Western, page 481, shows Shaft 7 at the corner of State Street and Eldridge Court (now 9th Street).  The 1906 Sanborn Map of Chicago (sheet 83s) shows the shaft on the south side of Eldridge just east of State.

gallery.title: File:IllinoisTunnelCongressFranklin.jpg
gallery.artist: George W. Jackson (died 1922)
gallery.description: Original Captions:  Western:  "Three-way Intersection at Congress and Franklin Streets." and inscribed along bottom:  "9148 4-27-02 Shaft No. 8 Congre ... [unreadable]"; Pages:  "THREE_WAY INTERSECTION AT CONGRESS AND FRANKLIN STREETS."  The captions are misleading; using the 1902 tunnel map as a reference, this must be a view west along Congress toward the intersection with Market St (now Wacker Dr.).  For scale, the track in the photos is 14 inch gauge.  The image is a composite of the two published sources to eliminate artifacts from printing and scanning.

gallery.title: File:IllinoisTunnelTrunkTunnelConstruction.jpg
gallery.artist: George W. Jackson (died 1922)
gallery.description: Original captions:  Western: "Fig. 8. "View of Trunk Conduit Under Construction." and inscribed on bottom of photo, "9182 Illinois Telephone and Telegraph Co. (illegible) Trunk System - Franklin & Washington Sts."   Pages: "Fig. 5. VIEW OF TRUNK CONDUIT UNDER CONSTRUCTION."  This image is a composite of both published versions in order to reduce artifacts from scanning and printing.  Trunk tunnels were 14 feet high by 12 3/4 feet wide.  The photo does not show the actual street intersection suggested in the title, but the system map in Western, Fig. 17, suggests that this section of trunk tunnel is near the base of Construction Shaft No. 3 on Franklin.  Since the shaft entrance is not in view, the camera must be facing north toward the street intersection.

gallery.description: Original Caption:  "Showing Conduits as Completed Sept 1. 1902."  Retouched to remove spots and improve legibility.  The short side spurs terminating in dots are the shafts used to construct the tunnel system.

gallery.title: File:IllinoisTunnelTestTrain.jpg
gallery.artist: Publicity photo taken by an anonymous photographer for the Illinois Tunnel Company
gallery.description: Original captions:  Trainman:  "THE CHICAGO UNDERGROUND ELECTRIC RAILWAY";  World: "A LOADED FREIGHT TRAIN FORTY FEET BELOW CHICAGO STREETS";  Independent:  "Loaded Trains in the Chicago Subway Tunnel"; Great Central Market: "LOADED FREIGHT TRAIN AT INTERSECTION"; Brownings (written on negative):  "(illegible) 1-2-04 Illinois Tunnel Co. Loaded Freight Train at Street Intersection";  System:  "The first freight ever carried below the streets of Chicago; the intersection of the tunnels at Congress Street and Wabash Avenue, showing freight in transit".-- This is one of the most widely printed and reprinted photos of the Chicago freight subway.  It is undoubtedly a test train since the system carried no commercial freight before 1905.  The cargo is probably cement barrels.  The tracks in the foreground are 14-inch gauge construction tracks.  With reference to the 1932 system map at the end of Bruce Moffat's book, Forty Feet Below, Interurban Press, 1982, the view must be looking north on Wabash with eastbound Congress to the right.

gallery.title: File:IllinoisTunnelFirstTrain.jpg
gallery.artist: Anonymous work for hire, probably hired by the Illinois Tunnel Company
gallery.description: Original caption:  "OPENING OF CHICAGO SUBWAY FOR FREIGHT TRAFFIC In the Chicago Milwaukee & St. Paul freight house, where the first train operated by the Illinois Tunnel Company was received."  On July 7, 1905, an 11 car train was dispatched over the 2-foot (61 cm) gauge tracks of the Illinois Tunnel Company from the Erie freight house.  These 5 cars were delivered to the Milwaukee freight house.  The elevator in the foreground goes down to the tunnel.
gallery.dateCreated: Taken on 15 July 1905; Published in 1910
